title: Daodejing, chapter 15 (Mawangdui silk manuscripts)
language: Classical Chinese (silk transcription; received text) / English
source: Mawangdui Laozi A and B silk manuscripts (plates of Changsha Mawangdui Han mu jianbo jicheng vol. 1, via Wikimedia Commons) + Wikisource column transcription + Wang Bi received text (Wikisource) + Legge 1891 English (Project Gutenberg)
description: Daodejing chapter 15 as written on the two Mawangdui silk manuscripts of the Laozi (before 168 BCE), with Legge's English and the received Chinese text.
introduction:
Chapter 15 of the Daodejing (Laozi), shown on the two oldest nearly complete copies of the work: the silk manuscripts Laozi A and Laozi B, found in 1973 in Tomb 3 at Mawangdui, Changsha (Hunan), a tomb sealed in 168 BCE. Laozi A is written in a script between seal and clerical forms and does not avoid the personal name of the Han founder Liu Bang (邦); it is commonly dated before 195 BCE. Laozi B is in clerical script, avoids 邦, and is commonly dated 194-180 BCE. Both put the De part (chapters 38-81) before the Dao part (chapters 1-37), and a few chapters stand in a different order from the received text.

Each section gives the silk transcription column by column, with the Jicheng column number before each column (for Laozi B, 上 and 下 are the upper and lower halves of a column, photographed on facing plates), and links to the plate that carries those columns. □ marks a lost character; ∠, ‧ and ﹦ are marks written on the silk (﹦ repeats the character before it). Below the transcription is the received text of the Wang Bi recension, which is the text James Legge translated in 1891; the silk wording differs from it, most visibly in 恆 for received 常 (the received text avoids the name of Emperor Wen, Liu Heng), in the frequent final particle 也, and in loan characters such as 胃 for 謂.
translator_notes: English: James Legge, The Tao Teh King (Sacred Books of the East 39, 1891); Legge's paragraph numbers are kept as superscripts.
Legge translated the received text, not the silk manuscripts. Where the silk wording differs, his English follows the received text shown under the transcription.
Silk transcription: Wikisource Page transcriptions of the Jicheng plates (revisions of 18 October 2026, marked not yet proofread on Wikisource), checked against the plates for each chapter opening.

translation.edition_text: 古之善為士者，微妙玄通，深不可識。夫唯不可識，故強為之容。豫焉若冬涉川，猶兮若畏四鄰，儼兮其若容，渙兮若冰之將釋，敦兮其若樸，曠兮其若谷，混兮其若濁。孰能濁以靜之徐清？孰能安以久動之徐生？保此道者不欲盈，夫唯不盈，故能蔽不新成。
translation.text:
1The skilful masters (of the Tao) in old times, with a subtle and exquisite penetration, comprehended its mysteries, and were deep (also) so as to elude men's knowledge. As they were thus beyond men's knowledge, I will make an effort to describe of what sort they appeared to be.

2Shrinking looked they like those who wade through a stream in winter; irresolute like those who are afraid of all around them; grave like a guest (in awe of his host); evanescent like ice that is melting away; unpretentious like wood that has not been fashioned into anything; vacant like a valley, and dull like muddy water.

3Who can (make) the muddy water (clear)? Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear. Who can secure the condition of rest? Let movement go on, and the condition of rest will gradually arise.

4They who preserve this method of the Tao do not wish to be full (of themselves). It is through their not being full of themselves that they can afford to seem worn and not appear new and complete.
translation.scan_note: Laozi A (甲本), columns 118 to 122, on plate p. 100 of Changsha Mawangdui Han mu jianbo jicheng, vol. 1 (column numbers are printed under each plate; the columns run from right to left). Checked on the image: column 119 reads 深不可志夫唯不可志故強為之容. The opening characters of this chapter are lost or not readable on this plate image, so these are the first characters that were confirmed. □ marks a character lost on the silk (31 in this section). Transcription and column numbers: Wikisource 老子 (帛書甲本), which follows the Jicheng column numbering. The English is Legge's translation of the received text, shown below the silk transcription; the silk wording differs from it in many places, so compare the two Chinese texts for the variants.
